statements.text: First, I'll touch on a few of the longer-term questions we're asking at the Fed about the latest general-purpose technology, artificial intelligence (AI), and where it might take the economy.

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: To cite the clearest example, progress in artificial intelligence—the 80-year-old name for the newest technology—has been faster even than its evangelists predicted a couple of years ago. The potential for substantially higher growth is on the rise. Ever-expanding pools of capital are pouring into AI-related infrastructure of all sorts.

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: Capital and labor have combined to create the large language models at the heart of AI. Users buy tokens to gain access to the models. Reports put annualized token sales for the two leading labs alone at more than $100 billion—an increase of 500-plus percent from a year ago.

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: We recognize that AI is a new variable—potentially a new factor of production—that will have consequences for both the economy and the conduct of monetary policy. It opens some major lines of inquiry: Will the application of AI cause a significant, sustained rise in productivity across the economy? And if so, when? Will token usage be complementary or competitive to labor? Will the next generation of AI models demand even greater capital intensity, or will the models themselves help devise a capital-light solution?

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: Early on, how much of the surplus goes to owners of scarce assets—AI labs, chipmakers, energy producers, and cloud providers? Over time, how much of that value accrues to businesses and consumers? What are the broad implications for workers and for the employment side of the Fed's mandate?

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: Likewise, we don't yet know the equilibrium price of the tokens. Might there be a heterogeneity of tokens, such that growing sums will be paid for access to the best models at the frontier? Will token prices for older models fall to the level of their marginal cost?

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: More than half of the cap-ex growth this year can likely be ascribed to the buildout related to AI.

attribution.speaker: Kevin Warsh
attribution.note: Automated extraction; exact quote and attribution span matched the retrieved source.

statements.text: The most striking feature of the economy right now is business investment. The rapid pace—which appears to be accelerating—reflects, in large part, the construction of data centers and the immense demand for the AI-related equipment and software that fill them.
